edits.target: ## Core workflow: compare options exactly, never pick by gist (follow even when answering quickly)
edits.content:
## Step 0 (do this FIRST, in writing): find the star-center of the options
Distractors are produced by single edits of the true statement, so the true statement is usually the center of a star. Before judging truth or strength:
(a) Split the options into atomic clauses and mark the shared skeleton.
(b) For each option, count how many OTHER options differ from it by exactly one clause. One-clause edits are: swap a constant, exponent, threshold or range; add or drop a rider; reverse a direction; weaken to a corollary; add a 'need not / only' hedge; replace a hypothesis.
(c) The option with the most one-edit neighbours is the CENTER and the default answer. If no option clearly has more neighbours (a chain, or two clusters), skip to the triage and workflow below.
(d) Override the center only with a concrete failing test on a named clause of the center (small case, degenerate case, count or dimension, scaling, finiteness, zero data). 'It feels too strong or too specific' and 'another option looks safer' are NOT failing tests. For a clause the center shares with its neighbours, 'I cannot derive it' alone is not a failing test either. For a clause that appears in only one option, derivation is required (see step 6).
(e) Never retreat to a leaf. Leaves include the strictly weaker true corollary, the one-direction version of an iff, 'only rational / only necessary', and 'need not hold' hedges. A leaf with an extra rider (an estimate, 'conversely every ... occurs', an explicit rate) is also a leaf.

## Triage (these filters override the 'safe' feeling; apply before the full workflow)
1. Strike options whose distinguishing clause is a limitation or negative: 'only ...', 'does not follow', 'need not / cannot', 'non-uniform', 'not FPT / only XP', 'the most one can conclude is ...', 'however ... has probability 0', 'once entered it can never leave', 'strictly larger kernel / extra non-obvious modes'. Source theorems are positive, so such tails are corruptions unless you can PROVE the negative. A stem hypothesis that is evidently there to enable a positive conclusion (a compatibility condition gives smoothness up to t=0; accessibility, step-size or dimension restrictions give global or full convergence) refutes an option saying that conclusion fails.
2. Self-consistency: an option's riders must not hollow out its own main claim. 'The process converges to one of several limits' plus 'all but one of them has probability 0' makes the 'one of' statement vacuous. The consistent version says each listed possibility genuinely occurs (positive probability).
3. Label every option in one word: truth / truncation (bare) / numeric inflation / negative hedge / paraphrase of another option. Choose the truth. A truncation loses to the truth whenever the extra clause is qualitative and derivable (see the bare-vs-rider test in step 6).
4. Existence/solvability stems with 'strongest': the plain positive theorem (existence, uniqueness, full regularity on the stated domain) beats any option that downgrades it to local-in-time, interior-only regularity, or 'not ensured'.

## Core workflow: compare options exactly, never pick by gist (follow even when answering quickly)

edits.target: 6. Do not default to the bare, minimal, or hedged option because it feels safe.
edits.content: 6. Do not default to the bare, minimal, or hedged option just because it feels safe. The opposite error is equally common: picking the option with the extra object, extra 'equivalently/moreover' gloss, higher index or level, or larger constant. Bare-vs-rider test: when option X = option Y + an extra clause, classify the clause. (a) Numeric or specific riders appearing in only one option (an explicit coefficient or second-order term, a sign claim such as V>V0, a rate, asymptotic closeness or boundedness for large t, a new object not named in the stem, a 'moreover' about specific values) are default-reject unless you can write a 2-line derivation. (b) Qualitative structural riders that are the natural content of the theorem and consistent with its mechanism (uniqueness for a well-posed problem, strict inequalities only off a plateau, positive probability for each possible limit, explicit constant dependence on the stem's parameters) are default-accept unless you find a counterexample. Never choose the bare option merely because you cannot verify a type-(b) clause, and never choose the rider option merely because it is longer. If you cannot justify a type-(a) extra, fall back to the plain theorem-level statement.

edits.target: The answer is the pivot between 'true but weaker' and 'sharper but unjustified'.
edits.content:
11. 'Equivalent to the assertion that ...' stems (reductions and gap theorems). The answer is normally a sibling of the stem's assertion with the same object type and the same property, changed in only one way that a named theorem justifies (a class reduced to a stem-defined subclass, or a bound tightened or collapsed). Check each option as follows.
   - Both directions. It must imply the stem's assertion and be implied by it. Shrinking the class of objects ('every N with an extra condition') gives a WEAKER statement that need not imply the original. Swapping the property for a weaker one (FFM→BFM, polylog→some bound) is not equivalent.
   - Vacuity test. Combine the hypotheses inside one option and see whether the class collapses. Example: if G(N)=G(M) already holds, then G(N)∩M=M, so adding 'G(N)∩M=N' forces N=M and the option says almost nothing. A rider that collapses or trivialises the class is the corruption.
   - Stem-defined terms. If the stem defines a special term (undermonoid, pseudovariety, a named class), the correct option usually uses that term plainly with the same target property. Options that re-spell the definition with extra conditions, or add named objects the stem never mentions (a forbidden-subsemigroup list, a vertex set X, a unit condition), are distractors.
   - Level matching. In logic and reverse-mathematics stems, the equivalent principle sits at the same complexity level as the objects in the stem (analytic = Sigma^1_1 ↔ Sigma^1_1 induction or separation). A level shifted up or down (Sigma^1_2, Pi^1_1) is an altered distractor.
   - Bound-sandwich stems. When the stem fixes a bound (e.g. O(log² N)) and options give a sharper and a weaker bound, determine which direction is the nontrivial theorem. Prefer the same-quantity sibling over a different-vocabulary structural characterization or width-restricted variants that add parameters.

edits.target: ## Near-duplicate options: constants, quantifiers, ranges, exact details
edits.content:
- Echoed stem constants and unit conversion: if an option reuses a number from the stem verbatim ('divides 2ℓ' when the stem says '2ℓ twists'), suspect it is the echo distractor. Convert units yourself (2ℓ half-twists = ℓ full twists, so the divisibility is by ℓ). Verify direction ('a divides ℓ' vs 'ℓ divides a') with one explicit small example.
- Conditions that look alike but depend on different data (an arithmetic condition on |A|, such as parity or 4∤|A|, vs a structural condition on a Sylow part, such as cyclic or elementary abelian): find the smallest examples where the options disagree (Z/2, Z/4, Z/2×Z/2, Z/3, Z/2×Z/3) and decide those cases directly. Do not accept an 'equivalently, exponent 2' style paraphrase unchecked.

edits.target: - If two options look equivalent under the stated ranges (e.g. 'm=2' vs 'm≡2 mod n' when 0≤m<n), re-read for a subtle difference. If they are truly equivalent, prefer the one in the problem's native modular or structural language.
edits.content: - Sibling-form tie-breaker: if several options share a syntactic form (all use congruences mod something, all use 'C=C(p,q,n)') and exactly one option uses a different but range-equivalent form ('=2' instead of '≡2 mod n'; 'some C>0' instead of 'C=C(p,q,n)'), that option is the odd one out. Do NOT pick it just because you proved it equivalent. Pick the sibling-form option that matches the source statement. For options identical except for constant dependence, the explicit dependence list on the stem's own parameters is the source formulation, and the bare 'some C>0' is the weakened version.

edits.target: be sceptical of any lower bound above the known record.
edits.content: If you cannot recall the exact record, look at the spacing of the numeric options. A tight cluster of nearly equal values (within about 1%) usually holds the previous record and the true new record, so pick the top of that cluster. Isolated values several percent or more above the cluster are inflated distractors, and values below it are weaker true statements. Do not choose a larger number just because 'a stronger bound is better' unless you can attest it.

edits.target: Options with specific numerics (explicit asymptotic coefficients, exact constants, extra sign or monotonicity claims, a 'moreover' clause on large-time behaviour) are the typical inflated distractors. Keep one only if you can derive the extra detail.
edits.content: A numeric, exponent or 'moreover' clause that appears in ONLY ONE option as an add-on (a sharper constant, an extra monotonicity or rate claim, a 'moreover' on large-time behaviour) is a typical inflated distractor. Keep it only if you can derive it. A specific numeric, threshold or formula that sits in the shared skeleton of several options (for example an awkward explicit threshold, a gcd-type formula, a weighted sum Σ c·N_c) is usually the authentic one. The distractors are the cleaner-looking substitutes: a round threshold like 2k, an exponent shifted to look natural, an unweighted sum, a formula with the key parameter dropped. When a clean substitute competes with an awkward specific version, test the clean one on a tiny case or a generic example (for example, ΣN_c<∞ with N_c≥1 forces finitely many c, which is false for a generic infinite spectrum) before choosing it.

edits.target: If the converse or realization claim is not derivable, it is an over-claim, not a strengthening.
edits.content: If the converse or realization claim is not derivable AND it appears as a rider on one option only (a leaf), it is an over-claim, not a strengthening. But if the iff or exact-formula form is the center of the options and the stem asks when something exists or for the exact value, it is the intended theorem. The one-direction version ('if it exists then ...'), 'the value is rational', and 'is a limit group' without the stated stronger property are then truncated leaves, even though they are true. A 'complete list of possible cases' stem asks only for the necessary list, and a 'conversely, every listed case occurs' rider is then a leaf.

edits.target: ## Using stem hypotheses as clues; odd-one-out swaps
edits.content: - Tailored-hypothesis stems: when the stem spells out an unusually specific conditional hypothesis (a case-specific side condition, an explicit numeric bound, a condition tied to one named prime, object, or index), treat it as the exact input of the source theorem. Options that relax it are corruptions unless you can prove the relaxation. Typical relaxations are broadening the class ('discrete series' for 'supercuspidal'), dropping part of the condition ('drop p≥5'), or decoupling it from the object it was imposed on ('some other prime, not necessarily the same one'). Phrases such as 'as soon as', 'even if', 'even without', and 'not necessarily' mark these. The winner is the plain option that states the strongest named conclusion under exactly the stem's hypotheses. It beats the weaker named property (a truncated version) and the relaxed-hypothesis versions (inflated ones).

- Structural-conflict test for riders: ask whether a rider contradicts a standard theorem or a model example in the stem's own setting. (a) A claim of a fixed or bounded ellipticity/constant together with a degenerate conclusion (exponent -> 0 exponentially, constants blowing up) contradicts compactness or De Giorgi-Nash-Moser type lower bounds. The valid version lets the ellipticity grow with the degeneracy parameter. (b) Regularity better than the optimal model behaviour (e.g. beyond C^s at a boundary where solutions behave like dist^s) is false. (c) 'Comes from a totally geodesic / subgroup-contained object' contradicts Zariski density or thinness. (d) A single object 'independent of the choice' contradicts the stem when the data varies. Reject the option the moment one such conflict is found, even if it looks sharper.

edits.target: A clause failing such a check is the corruption.
edits.content: - Container and definedness checks: compare dim(object) with dim(container). A closed manifold cannot sit inside a same-dimensional proper totally geodesic subsphere, so 'lies in an equator of dimension equal to its own' fails, and 'embeds in the sphere of its own dimension' fails for a non-sphere. Check whether an 'everywhere-defined regular morphism' claim is compatible with a non-constant invariant on a projective or complete base (a Grassmannian with Picard rank 1 admits no non-constant map to P^1). Then only a rational map, with indeterminacy locus, is available, and the 'regular' option is the corruption. Dropping a non-essential rider (e.g. 'invariant' vs 'invariant plus fibre structure') should leave the plain statement.

edits.target: ## Strength calibration (two-sided): the answer must be true AND maximal
edits.content: - Standard rungs and typical inflations. Familiar hierarchies: ergodic < weakly mixing < strongly mixing; '→0' or n^{1/2+o(1)} < O(f) with the natural base and exponent < O(f) with a smaller base, exponent or shaved log < ~K·f with an explicit constant (this needs a matching lower bound, which upper-bound theorems rarely have); 'dim > 0' < 'dim ≥ explicit c' < 'dim ≥ larger c'. Pick the rung a paper would state as its main theorem. Reject three inflations unless derivable: (a) form change, where the stem defines a quantity (a liminf exponent, a limsup) and an option restates it as a pointwise constant-form bound (c·N^a for all large N), which is strictly stronger; (b) added uniformity, where an 'absolute constant' or 'for every α' replaces the stem's fixed-parameter statement; (c) a changed relation or exponent (< or ≥ instead of =, a sharper base such as 3^n for 4^n). When displayed numerics agree with their closed forms (logarithm base, denominators), decide by the differing constant or exponent against the source theorem.

edits.target: - Reject options that restrict to one test vector or special case when the stem asks for a general statement, and options that add an existence or 'conversely' claim when the base statement already answers the question.
edits.content:
- Recipe riders: clauses saying HOW the object is built or WHAT it uses ('only from a metric on the base', 'with only finitely many correction terms', 'without any auxiliary data', 'can always be obtained from ...') are inflated or altered corruptions unless derivable. The faithful claim states the object and its defining property ('an explicit metric inducing exactly the stated topology'). That claim still beats a bare 'is metrizable / exists' when the construction is standard from the stem's data, since the stronger clause is derivable. Likewise, do not add a regime or class restriction ('provided the parameters are distinct') that the stem's hypotheses do not need.
- Formula-variant options (same equation, different coefficients, sum ranges or solution-count wording): list the options as single edits of one hub. Typical edits are a halved vs full term, odd l vs all l, 'only one' vs 'at most one', and the same weight on two types. Do not prefer the more symmetric or tidier formula. If the stem treats two types differently (e.g. Type O vs Type I), expect different coefficients. 'Has only one solution' is the natural uniqueness phrasing when existence is built into the data, so 'at most one' is a hedge, not the safer answer. Confirm the coefficient with a one-block or one-dimensional sanity case.

## Leaf traps seen in practice (each wrong pick was one of these; the right answer was the center)
- Cleaner-hypothesis gloss ('the explicit threshold can be replaced by d>2k'), a swapped threshold type ('there exists some D(k)'), a dropped-simplicity claim, or a sharper constant (≤5 for ≤6) are leaves of the explicit-threshold center.
- Estimate rider: when the stem gives data with a lower-order unknown and asks for 'the strongest statement about every such h', the plain regularity membership is the center. A bound of ||h|| by the data norms alone fails the zero-data test (h need not vanish), so it is a leaf.
- Exponent shifts in asymptotics: use the stem's threshold (γ>1) and the form of the center. Prefer the exponent that is natural and decaying exactly on the stem's range (u^{-(γ-1)} needs γ>1). Do not import a template such as 'Kesten u^{-γ}'. A '~ C u^{-a}' center beats its O(·), ε-loss and complementary-probability variants.
- Hedge leaf: an option saying a property 'need not hold when q≠0' while another option asserts that property is a direct contradiction. Decide the property itself. If it is the natural companion of the other stated conclusions, as 'fully residually free' is of 'limit group', the hedge is false.
- Weighted-sum leaf: 'ΣN_c<∞' versus 'Σ c·N_c<∞' for positive-integer multiplicities. Only the weighted form allows infinitely many velocities, which is the generic case.
- Exact-formula leaf: when the stem says 'which exact statement holds for every p', test the candidate formulas on a tiny case or a degenerate parameter (for example m=n, gcd=1, one anchor). The formula that survives, not the vague 'it is rational' corollary, is the answer.
- Classification/rigidity leaf: if one option says the Jacobi fields, kernel or modes are 'exactly the obvious/symmetry-generated ones' and another claims a strictly larger space with 'non-obvious' elements, the larger claim needs a dimension or eigenvalue count you can check. An option saying only 'every Killing field is a Jacobi field' is a truncation of the full classification.

## List-membership options ('exactly the candidates that hold, the others fail')
- Write each option as a set of items. Items common to all options need no work. Only the symmetric difference between options decides the answer, so test those items one at a time.
- Test each differing item with extremal or degenerate examples (a regular graph, a star, a complete graph, a path, n=1 or n=2). A single counterexample refutes 'holds'. A proof, or domination by an item already known to hold (pointwise ≤ a valid bound), supports it. Check consistency: if one formula is pointwise ≤ a valid one, its membership must match.
- A 'for exactly these' stem needs both halves, 'these hold' and 'the others fail for some instance'. The option that states only the 'hold' half is a truncation, so prefer the option that gives both halves and gets every differing item right.
